content: Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic used to treat a wide range of bacterial infections. It may also be prescribed to prevent certain bacterial infections. This medication is effective only against bacterial infections and will not work for viral infections such as the common cold or flu. Administration Instructions: Take erythromycin orally as directed by your physician, typically before a meal. It is best absorbed on an empty stomach. Do not crush the medication, as it has a bitter taste; swallow it whole. The dosage and duration of treatment depend on your medical condition and response to therapy. For optimal results, take the medication at evenly spaced intervals. If prescribed for an infection, complete the full course of treatment, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Stopping the medication prematurely may result in a recurrence of the infection. If using erythromycin to prevent infections, follow your doctor’s instructions precisely. Common Side Effects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain or cramping, and loss of appetite may occur. Taking the medication with food may help alleviate these symptoms. This medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Rare but Serious Side Effects: Erythromycin may rarely cause a severe intestinal condition due to the bacteria Clostridium difficile (C. difficile). This condition can occur during treatment or weeks to months after stopping the medication. Prolonged or repeated use of erythromycin may lead to oral thrush or a new yeast infection. Severe allergic reactions to this drug are rare but possible. Precautions: Inform your doctor if you are allergic to erythromycin, other macrolide antibiotics (e.g., azithromycin, clarithromycin), or any other substances. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other problems. Erythromycin may cause a condition affecting the heart rhythm known as QT prolongation. The risk of QT prolongation may increase if you have certain medical conditions or are taking other drugs that can cause QT prolongation. Low levels of potassium or magnesium in the blood may also increase the risk of QT prolongation. This risk may be heightened if you are using certain medications (e.g., diuretics) or have conditions such as severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting. Drug Interactions: Drug interactions may alter how your medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. Erythromycin can slow the removal of other drugs from your body, potentially affecting how they work. It may interfere with certain lab tests (e.g., urine tests), possibly causing false results. Overdose: In the event of an overdose with serious symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call emergency services immediately (911 in the U.S.). Otherwise, contact a poison control center right away. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222. Missed Dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is near the time of the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular dosing schedule. Do not double the dose to catch up. Storage: Store erythromycin at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. Pregnancy and Lactation: Erythromycin is classified as Pregnancy Category B, meaning that controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk. This medication is distributed in breast milk. Use with caution while breastfeeding. The American Academy of Pediatrics categorizes erythromycin as compatible with breastfeeding. Important Notes: Prolonged or repeated use of erythromycin may result in the overgrowth of non-susceptible bacteria or fungi. If superinfection occurs, discontinue erythromycin and initiate appropriate therapy. In cases where indicated, surgical procedures such as incision and drainage should be performed alongside antibiotic therapy. Observational studies in humans have reported cardiovascular malformations after exposure to erythromycin-containing drug products during early pregnancy. Erythromycin is primarily excreted by the liver. Exercise caution when administering it to patients with impaired hepatic function. Exacerbation of symptoms of myasthenia gravis and new onset of myasthenic syndrome symptoms have been reported in patients receiving erythromycin therapy. This information is not exhaustive and does not replace professional medical advice. Always consult your healthcare provider for complete information about this product and your specific health needs.
